Shadow king: the Bakgatla story

By: Anina Peens | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
When greed crowned a traitor, the richest tribe in South Africa lost its king—and its future

Unique Selling Point:
This is a story of murder, corruption, and billions spent on private assets—of a tribal king forced into exile, and a community living in abject poverty, powerless as one of their own enriches national and regional elites.

Summary:
In South Africa’s platinum-rich north, the Bakgatla ba Kgafela people were once poised to be one of the wealthiest traditional communities in the country.
While billions flowed from mines and luxury resorts built on their land, the community sank into poverty. The money was siphoned off by politically connected elites—led by a tribal appointee who betrayed the crown and enriched himself. Whistleblowers were murdered. The rightful king was forced into exile
Now, with help from private prosecutors, the Bakgatla are fighting to reclaim their land, expose corruption, and restore what was stolen from them in plain sight.

Further information:
For centuries, the Tswana people of the North West have lived at the foot of the Pilanesberg mountains. The name “Pilanesberg” itself is derived from their first tribal king, Pilane. During the mid-1800s, when the Voortrekkers arrived in the region, a period of peaceful coexistence followed. The Boers and the Bakgatla people protected each other, with the Boers helping to safeguard livestock while the Bakgatla offered shelter and support.
When King Pilane died, his son Kgamanyane succeeded him. Around the same time, a young farmer and field cornet of the British colonial government—Paul Kruger—clashed with Kgamanyane. The fallout was severe enough that the young king was forced to migrate north toward what is now Botswana. Some members of the tribe followed him, while others remained behind. Those who stayed were assigned a local leader (Kgosi) to oversee their affairs, but this leader continued to report to the king in exile.
After the fall of apartheid in 1994, the homeland of Bophuthatswana—of which Bakgatla land formed a part—was dissolved and its territories absorbed into the new democratic South Africa. The ANC government encouraged traditional communities like the Bakgatla to relinquish self-rule in favor of integration into provincial structures. The Bakgatla leadership agreed, on the understanding that their economic development would be managed transparently through these new governmental systems.
But thirty years later, many in the community feel betrayed. Promises of prosperity have not materialized. Instead, they argue that they are worse off now than ever before. Disillusioned with the local municipality, which they believe does not represent their interests, the Bakgatla want to reclaim their right to self-govern. The major obstacle, however, is that the land they occupy legally belongs to the state. Any defiance could risk eviction. They have been requesting title deeds for years, but the government has not acted—allegedly because doing so would mean losing control over a significant voter base. If the people rule themselves, the ANC’s political influence over the region diminishes.
What sets the Bakgatla apart from other impoverished rural communities is that they are sitting on vast natural wealth. If given access to and control over their land, they could become one of the richest traditional communities in the country.
Meanwhile, another complication has emerged. The king in Botswana—descended from Kgamanyane—appointed a family member, also named Pilane, to lead the Bakgatla on the South African side. But once money entered the equation, Pilane broke ranks with the king and enriched himself.
The first major controversy involved the Union Mine, a platinum operation located on Bakgatla land. Community members allege that Pilane embezzled funds meant for the tribe. Today, he and his nephew are implicated in a new scheme tied to the Siyanda Bakgatla Platinum Mine. Land, originally held in trust or under state custodianship, was sold to the mining operation. Pilane’s nephew now sits on the board of Siyanda Bakgatla Platinum Mine. Both he and Pilane are also directors of Bakgatla Investment Holdings—the company responsible for managing the community’s share of mining profits. This creates an evident conflict of interest. Despite promises of dividends and development, the money has failed to reach the people.

The community has not remained silent. They wrote directly to former Minister of Agriculture, Land Reform, and Rural Development, Thoko Didiza. She acknowledged that the land in question should be returned to the community. While some tracts have been handed over, the most lucrative areas remain withheld—namely those involving mining operations, luxury lodges such as Kwa Maritane and Red Ivory, and high-value assets like Sun City. These properties continue to generate revenue, but the Bakgatla people see none of it.
The central question that remains unanswered is this: How did Siyanda Bakgatla Platinum Mine legally acquire land that was supposed to belong to the Bakgatla people? And why is the state silent, despite written acknowledgement of the tribe’s rightful claims?

SHADOW KING: THE BAKGATLA STORY FINAL SCRIPT
(GRACE MALEDU) I grew up here, and I know this land as much as I know myself. Without the land, there is no life.
(ERIN BATES) Now 77, Grace Maledu has spent much of her life fighting for rights to a farm her family bought more than a century ago.
(GRACE MALEDU) I know how to make honey I know how to make butter because we were milking 25 liters per day in the morning and the afternoon and make ourselves inkomasi, I know how to do this because of the land.
(ERIN BATES) In the mid- 2000s, everything changed when a mining company eyed the same farm… or rather the minerals beneath it—some of the most valuable on earth. Wilgespruit Farm is just one of many belonging to the Bakgatla ba Kgafela, a Tswana tribe in the North West. The tribe is spread across 32 villages on over 300- thousand hectares of land at the foothills of the Pilansberg.
(GRACE MALEDU) Those people who are misusing our land, it because it is not their land. It’s not their land, they don’t feel for it.
(ERIN BATES) In the 1800s, some villages pooled their money to buy farms. Grace says her forefathers paid for Wilgespruit around 1916.
(GRACE MALEDU)
I love this land so much, even when I speak like this, I saw my grandparents in front of me and I know how they lived in this land
(ERIN BATES) In 1994, the newly elected government took control of the farms, declaring them “communal land”. Now, the Bakgatla wants them back.
(ALLAN FEW) We then got an old map from 1905 which was a hand drawn map and from that we then identified the area we were looking at. We then went and pulled new maps.
(ERIN BATES) Forensic investigator, Allen Few, has spent years tracing the Bakgatla’s land claims.
(ALLAN FEW) The government is not forthcoming with the title deeds. We have got letters dated 2006, 2008, 2010, 2020 which the land is promised back to them by the government, the government says, your land claim has been successful and we are gonna give you your title deeds. To give you and example, the farm Doringhoek, 910JQ 72 where Sun city is sitting, we have got a letter from the government to say that farm must be returned to them
(ERIN BATES) Allan found a signed document dating back to the 1800s in which community members who contributed to buying farms are listed. Those names are etched in headstones across village graveyards.
(ERIN BATES) The Bakgatla bought their land fair and square, many of them are buried here…But the battle for true ownership is very much alive.
(ERIN BATES) With no rights to their land, mines can move in with a state licence and the chief’s signature. The chief, known as the Kgosi, calls the shots.
(KGOSI JOHN MOLEFE ‘NYALALA’ PILANE) My name is Kgosi Molefe John Pilane but popularly known as Nyalala.
(ERIN BATES) Nyalala was appointed in 1996.
(KGOSI JOHN MOLEFE ‘NYALALA’ PILANE) Once you have been identified by the royal family then the premier must acknowledge after he or she has been informed by the royal body, that this is the person who must now start to liaise with government on our behalf.
(ERIN BATES) And that relationship is at the heart of a decades long battle over land and mining rights as Nyalala is alleged to have struck multi billion rand deals using the community’s land. Lawyer Henk Smith has been helping Grace and the community reclaim their rights to the farm Wilgespruit.
(HENK SMIT: LAWYER) The mining right in the Wilgespruit farm was obtained by a mining company called IBMR- Itireng Bakgatla mining / mineral resources company. That mining company was owned by the chief himself. 17:57:14:16 The state promptly awarded the right to the Nyalala and his company [DM1] .
(GRACE MALEDU) They just make agreements without us. We will see it from the papers and see it from TV.
(ERIN BATES) The mining right was first granted to Itereleng Bakgatla Mineral Resources, a company run by the Traditional Council, and later transferred to a private mining company. It is here where the community says they were blindsided.
(ERIN BATES) With the chief’s signature, the mines started operations and life became unbearable for Grace and her community. When they went to court to stop the mine, they were thrown off their own land.
(GRACE MALEDU) We want the soil, that is why we went to concourt, we want the soil, back to our hands so we can use it as we want.
(ERIN BATES) Grace took the battle to the constitutional court and won. Not only that, but a legal precedent was also set demanding that mines consult with communities. But it was a short-lived victory.
(HENK SMIT) They’re trying their luck over and over and the department is playing along
(ERIN BATES) In July, despite the Con Court judgement, the very same mine, applied for a new license to expand onto her beloved Wilgespruit. The community responded by protesting outside the Department of Mineral Resources.
(HENK SMIT) Now there is a new mining right application it should’ve been reviewed and set aside. The same mining company is making the same mistakes and not following the procedures of the law.
(ERIN BATES) The community is at loggerheads with Nyalala and the provincial government over Wilgespruit, but others are also impacted. In surrounding villages, anger mounts as mining on community land is seen to benefit only Nyalala.
(LEBOGANG MANANE) What happened is land expropriation without compensation. Before it was legislated. And that is crime. You cannot take our land without our consent.
(ERIN BATES) At a meeting in a neighbouring village, community leader, Lebogang Manane, raised concerns about the way deals are done without their knowledge.
(LEBOGANG MANANE)Instead of the Bakgatla ba Kgafela being the direct beneficiaries, he uses companies to own on behalf of Bakgatla ba Kgafela and he becomes a sole director.
(ERIN BATES) Allan’s investigation revealed eye watering amounts moving into these companies in royalties from mining deals.
(ALLAN FEW) Half of the stuff he did, the community doesn’t know about it. Everything was done through a private company.
(ALLAN FEW) There was a company called Lexshelf 703 PTY ltd, all the dividends from mines went into that account and in the period that that account was running, one point three billion Rand disappeared.
(ERIN BATES) In 2019, a commission set up to probe the flow of money in and out of the community, exposed how Nyalala and his family were allegedly benefiting from a web of companies. It was called the Baloyi Inquiry and, when challenged in court by Nyalala, its findings were overturned on a technicality.
(HENK SMIT) Any challenge that goes to the Northwest high court. So many wrong decisions come from that court.
(ERIN BATES) But, in 2022, a report by the Department of Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs made similar findings to the Baloyi Commission.
(ERIN BATES) But that didn’t stop government from giving Nyalala another certificate of recognition as chief – much to the community’s anger.
(LEBOGANG MANANE) Nyalala is being protected by Politicians, you can see him, its clear.
(ERIN BATES) Nyalala didn’t want to comment on any of the Baloi findings.
(NYALALA PILANE) It was overturned and the reason for that is I’m sure you know is because it was wrong, it cannot be overturned if it was correct.
(ERIN BATES) The allegation is that you are skimming off the fat off mining companies, you are warding off land claims in order to further the interest of private business. You are costing your people.
(NYALALA PILANE) Well, its an allegation. What do you want me to do?
(ERIN BATES) But beyond the mines, land access, and a divided community, Nyalala faces another challenge: a large faction of his people claim he is an illegitimate Kgosi. In the shadows of this story is another leader, vying for the throne, insisting he is the rightful king of the Bakgatla.
( KGOSI KGOLO KGAFELA KGAFELA) everybody knows within my tribe, that the king has been forced out of the tribal office not only the office but out of his home and his village by a mob that is ANC sponsored.
(ERIN BATES) Kgosi Kgafela Kgafela II is by blood the king of the Bakgatla. His forefathers moved to Botswana in the late 1800s, and the tribe remained united under the monarchy. It’s this royal family who appointed Nyalala as the king’s representative in 1996.
( KGOSI KGOLO KGAFELA KGAFELA) You’re looking at a tradition that has lasted from 1870. Only the king can appoint a representative in South Africa. He was appointed by my father and when I took over from my father, I had the prerogative will I continue with him or not. I continued with him from 2008, 2009, 11 we were together.
(ERIN BATES) But relations soured as allegations against Nyalala mounted.
( KGOSI KGOLO KGAFELA KGAFELA:) There is this force that is destroying Bagatla. 11:34:54:37 the evidence is more than compelling to start an investigation yesterday.
(ERIN BATES) Kgafela blames the ANC for keeping Nyalala in power.
( KGOSI KGOLO KGAFELA KGAFELA) We had forensic report after forensic report…reports pointing towards one conclusion that Pilane is committing serious crimes against Bagatla Ba Kgafela.
(ERIN BATES) While the government acknowledges it was Kgafela’s father who made Nyalala chief, they don’t recognise Kgafela’s right to remove him. That, they claim, is because Kgafela was born in Botswana and has no authority in South Africa.
( KGOSI KGOLO KGAFELA KGAFELA) The ANC what they do is they frustrate the legitimate traditional leader. They break his ability to lead his people and in his place they put their cadre, someone that they know will give them tribal money. Somebody who they know will steal from the tribe and play their game of corruption
(ERIN BATES) The North West premier’s office dismisses these claims as baseless, and Nyalala says, Kgafela is a one man band with no power.
(NYALALA PILANE) He is not a king. He is not a traditional leader and neither is he a king in South Africa. He is a Kgosi in Botswana.
(ERIN BATES) Kgafela has been in exile in the Western Cape since last year, after one of his close allies in the land and mining battle was murdered under suspicious circumstance. The man had deep knowledge of land disputes and the flow of the mining royalties.
( KGOSI KGOLO KGAFELA KGAFELA) A colleague of mine has been shot, and we know who did it but they haven’t been arrested and that is not the only one, people are being shot in my tribe.
( KGOSI KGOLO KGAFELA KGAFELA) The future is too precious for me to take the risk of being around North West. They will murder anyone who stands in their way.
(ERIN BATES) Meanwhile, community members say the monarchy isn’t up for debate, it’s rooted in centuries of history and tradition.
(LEBOGANG MANANE) Kgosi Kgafela Kgafela is our king. Is like maybe you are saying to me I have a choice as to whose my parents. My mother will always be my mother. 15:34:57:25 We need our king back. We need to be led by our king.
(ERIN BATES) The Bakgatla case highlights the gap between promises of land reform and actual delivery; one apparently predicated on the idea that the most valuable land should stay out of community hands.
(ALLAN FEW ) It’s a smokescreen…If the government actually have to give back what the people have already claimed and what was rightfully theirs, we wouldn’t be having this discussion.

(ERIN BATES) With no rights to their land, mines can move in with a state licence and the chief’s signature. The chief, known as the Kgosi, calls the shots. (KGOSI JOHN MOLEFE ‘NYALALA’ PILANE) My name is Kgosi Molefe John Pilane but popularly known as Nyalala. (ERIN BATES) Nyalala was appointed in 1996. (KGOSI JOHN MOLEFE ‘NYALALA’ PILANE) Once you have been identified by the royal family then the premier must acknowledge after he or she has been informed by the royal body, that this is the person who must now start to liaise with government on our behalf. (ERIN BATES) And that relationship is at the heart of a decades long battle over land and mining rights as Nyalala is alleged to have struck multi billion rand deals using the community’s land. Lawyer Henk Smith has been helping Grace and the community reclaim their rights to the farm Wilgespruit. (HENK SMIT: LAWYER) The mining right in the Wilgespruit farm was obtained by a mining company called IBMR- Itireng Bakgatla mining / mineral resources company. That mining company was owned by the chief himself. 17:57:14:16 The state promptly awarded the right to the Nyalala and his company [DM1] . (GRACE MALEDU) They just make agreements without us. We will see it from the papers and see it from TV. (ERIN BATES) The mining right was first granted to Itereleng Bakgatla Mineral Resources, a company run by the Traditional Council, and later transferred to a private mining company. It is here where the community says they were blindsided. (ERIN BATES) With the chief’s signature, the mines started operations and life became unbearable for Grace and her community. When they went to court to stop the mine, they were thrown off their own land. (GRACE MALEDU) We want the soil, that is why we went to concourt, we want the soil, back to our hands so we can use it as we want. (ERIN BATES) Grace took the battle to the constitutional court and won. Not only that, but a legal precedent was also set demanding that mines consult with communities. But it was a short-lived victory. (HENK SMIT) They’re trying their luck over and over and the department is playing along (ERIN BATES) In July, despite the Con Court judgement, the very same mine, applied for a new license to expand onto her beloved Wilgespruit. The community responded by protesting outside the Department of Mineral Resources. (HENK SMIT) Now there is a new mining right application it should’ve been reviewed and set aside. The same mining company is making the same mistakes and not following the procedures of the law. (ERIN BATES) The community is at loggerheads with Nyalala and the provincial government over Wilgespruit, but others are also impacted. In surrounding villages, anger mounts as mining on community land is seen to benefit only Nyalala. (LEBOGANG MANANE) What happened is land expropriation without compensation. Before it was legislated. And that is crime. You cannot take our land without our consent. (ERIN BATES) At a meeting in a neighbouring village, community leader, Lebogang Manane, raised concerns about the way deals are done without their knowledge. (LEBOGANG MANANE)Instead of the Bakgatla ba Kgafela being the direct beneficiaries, he uses companies to own on behalf of Bakgatla ba Kgafela and he becomes a sole director. (ERIN BATES) Allan’s investigation revealed eye watering amounts moving into these companies in royalties from mining deals. (ALLAN FEW) Half of the stuff he did, the community doesn’t know about it. Everything was done through a private company. (ALLAN FEW) There was a company called Lexshelf 703 PTY ltd, all the dividends from mines went into that account and in the period that that account was running, one point three billion Rand disappeared. (ERIN BATES) In 2019, a commission set up to probe the flow of money in and out of the community, exposed how Nyalala and his family were allegedly benefiting from a web of companies. It was called the Baloyi Inquiry and, when challenged in court by Nyalala, its findings were overturned on a technicality. (HENK SMIT) Any challenge that goes to the Northwest high court. So many wrong decisions come from that court. (ERIN BATES) But, in 2022, a report by the Department of Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs made similar findings to the Baloyi Commission. (ERIN BATES) But that didn’t stop government from giving Nyalala another certificate of recognition as chief – much to the community’s anger. (LEBOGANG MANANE) Nyalala is being protected by Politicians, you can see him, its clear. (ERIN BATES) Nyalala didn’t want to comment on any of the Baloi findings. (NYALALA PILANE) It was overturned and the reason for that is I’m sure you know is because it was wrong, it cannot be overturned if it was correct. (ERIN BATES) The allegation is that you are skimming off the fat off mining companies, you are warding off land claims in order to further the interest of private business. You are costing your people. (NYALALA PILANE) Well, its an allegation. What do you want me to do? (ERIN BATES) But beyond the mines, land access, and a divided community, Nyalala faces another challenge: a large faction of his people claim he is an illegitimate Kgosi. In the shadows of this story is another leader, vying for the throne, insisting he is the rightful king of the Bakgatla. ( KGOSI KGOLO KGAFELA KGAFELA) everybody knows within my tribe, that the king has been forced out of the tribal office not only the office but out of his home and his village by a mob that is ANC sponsored. (ERIN BATES) Kgosi Kgafela Kgafela II is by blood the king of the Bakgatla. His forefathers moved to Botswana in the late 1800s, and the tribe remained united under the monarchy. It’s this royal family who appointed Nyalala as the king’s representative in 1996. ( KGOSI KGOLO KGAFELA KGAFELA) You’re looking at a tradition that has lasted from 1870. Only the king can appoint a representative in South Africa. He was appointed by my father and when I took over from my father, I had the prerogative will I continue with him or not. I continued with him from 2008, 2009, 11 we were together. (ERIN BATES) But relations soured as allegations against Nyalala mounted. ( KGOSI KGOLO KGAFELA KGAFELA:) There is this force that is destroying Bagatla. 11:34:54:37 the evidence is more than compelling to start an investigation yesterday. (ERIN BATES) Kgafela blames the ANC for keeping Nyalala in power. ( KGOSI KGOLO KGAFELA KGAFELA) We had forensic report after forensic report…reports pointing towards one conclusion that Pilane is committing serious crimes against Bagatla Ba Kgafela. (ERIN BATES) While the government acknowledges it was Kgafela’s father who made Nyalala chief, they don’t recognise Kgafela’s right to remove him. That, they claim, is because Kgafela was born in Botswana and has no authority in South Africa. ( KGOSI KGOLO KGAFELA KGAFELA) The ANC what they do is they frustrate the legitimate traditional leader. They break his ability to lead his people and in his place they put their cadre, someone that they know will give them tribal money. Somebody who they know will steal from the tribe and play their game of corruption (ERIN BATES) The North West premier’s office dismisses these claims as baseless, and Nyalala says, Kgafela is a one man band with no power. (NYALALA PILANE) He is not a king. He is not a traditional leader and neither is he a king in South Africa. He is a Kgosi in Botswana. (ERIN BATES) Kgafela has been in exile in the Western Cape since last year, after one of his close allies in the land and mining battle was murdered under suspicious circumstance. The man had deep knowledge of land disputes and the flow of the mining royalties. ( KGOSI KGOLO KGAFELA KGAFELA) A colleague of mine has been shot, and we know who did it but they haven’t been arrested and that is not the only one, people are being shot in my tribe. ( KGOSI KGOLO KGAFELA KGAFELA) The future is too precious for me to take the risk of being around North West. They will murder anyone who stands in their way. (ERIN BATES) Meanwhile, community members say the monarchy isn’t up for debate, it’s rooted in centuries of history and tradition. (LEBOGANG MANANE) Kgosi Kgafela Kgafela is our king. Is like maybe you are saying to me I have a choice as to whose my parents. My mother will always be my mother. 15:34:57:25 We need our king back. We need to be led by our king. (ERIN BATES) The Bakgatla case highlights the gap between promises of land reform and actual delivery; one apparently predicated on the idea that the most valuable land should stay out of community hands. (ALLAN FEW ) It’s a smokescreen…If the government actually have to give back what the people have already claimed and what was rightfully theirs, we wouldn’t be having this discussion.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): When greed crowned a traitor, the richest tribe in South Africa lost its king—and its future
metadata.Unique Selling Point: This is a story of murder, corruption, and billions spent on private assets—of a tribal king forced into exile, and a community living in abject poverty, powerless as one of their own enriches national and regional elites.
metadata.Summary: In South Africa’s platinum-rich north, the Bakgatla ba Kgafela people were once poised to be one of the wealthiest traditional communities in the country. While billions flowed from mines and luxury resorts built on their land, the community sank into poverty. The money was siphoned off by politically connected elites—led by a tribal appointee who betrayed the crown and enriched himself. Whistleblowers were murdered. The rightful king was forced into exile Now, with help from private prosecutors, the Bakgatla are fighting to reclaim their land, expose corruption, and restore what was stolen from them in plain sight.
metadata.Further information: For centuries, the Tswana people of the North West have lived at the foot of the Pilanesberg mountains. The name “Pilanesberg” itself is derived from their first tribal king, Pilane. During the mid-1800s, when the Voortrekkers arrived in the region, a period of peaceful coexistence followed. The Boers and the Bakgatla people protected each other, with the Boers helping to safeguard livestock while the Bakgatla offered shelter and support. When King Pilane died, his son Kgamanyane succeeded him. Around the same time, a young farmer and field cornet of the British colonial government—Paul Kruger—clashed with Kgamanyane. The fallout was severe enough that the young king was forced to migrate north toward what is now Botswana. Some members of the tribe followed him, while others remained behind. Those who stayed were assigned a local leader (Kgosi) to oversee their affairs, but this leader continued to report to the king in exile. After the fall of apartheid in 1994, the homeland of Bophuthatswana—of which Bakgatla land formed a part—was dissolved and its territories absorbed into the new democratic South Africa. The ANC government encouraged traditional communities like the Bakgatla to relinquish self-rule in favor of integration into provincial structures. The Bakgatla leadership agreed, on the understanding that their economic development would be managed transparently through these new governmental systems. But thirty years later, many in the community feel betrayed. Promises of prosperity have not materialized. Instead, they argue that they are worse off now than ever before. Disillusioned with the local municipality, which they believe does not represent their interests, the Bakgatla want to reclaim their right to self-govern. The major obstacle, however, is that the land they occupy legally belongs to the state. Any defiance could risk eviction. They have been requesting title deeds for years, but the government has not acted—allegedly because doing so would mean losing control over a significant voter base. If the people rule themselves, the ANC’s political influence over the region diminishes. What sets the Bakgatla apart from other impoverished rural communities is that they are sitting on vast natural wealth. If given access to and control over their land, they could become one of the richest traditional communities in the country. Meanwhile, another complication has emerged. The king in Botswana—descended from Kgamanyane—appointed a family member, also named Pilane, to lead the Bakgatla on the South African side. But once money entered the equation, Pilane broke ranks with the king and enriched himself. The first major controversy involved the Union Mine, a platinum operation located on Bakgatla land. Community members allege that Pilane embezzled funds meant for the tribe. Today, he and his nephew are implicated in a new scheme tied to the Siyanda Bakgatla Platinum Mine. Land, originally held in trust or under state custodianship, was sold to the mining operation. Pilane’s nephew now sits on the board of Siyanda Bakgatla Platinum Mine. Both he and Pilane are also directors of Bakgatla Investment Holdings—the company responsible for managing the community’s share of mining profits. This creates an evident conflict of interest. Despite promises of dividends and development, the money has failed to reach the people. The community has not remained silent. They wrote directly to former Minister of Agriculture, Land Reform, and Rural Development, Thoko Didiza. She acknowledged that the land in question should be returned to the community. While some tracts have been handed over, the most lucrative areas remain withheld—namely those involving mining operations, luxury lodges such as Kwa Maritane and Red Ivory, and high-value assets like Sun City. These properties continue to generate revenue, but the Bakgatla people see none of it. The central question that remains unanswered is this: How did Siyanda Bakgatla Platinum Mine legally acquire land that was supposed to belong to the Bakgatla people? And why is the state silent, despite written acknowledgement of the tribe’s rightful claims?
